title: Son of Adam (Luke 3:15–38)
hook: after the baptism, Luke traces Jesus back past Abraham, to Adam, son of God
carry: son of adam, son of god

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crowds at the Jordan asking John what shall we do, and his answer: share your coat. Did one thing you had two of find a new home? Day five hundred fourteen.

Luke's family tree runs the wrong way. A family tree usually starts with the oldest name and works down to the youngest. Luke starts with Jesus, about thirty years old, and climbs. Son of Joseph, as was supposed. Son of Heli. Son of Matthat. Back through King David, back through Abraham, back past the flood to Noah, and still he keeps going. Dozens of names, a long ladder of fathers that's easy to skip. But it's worth reading to the very last rung, because of where Luke puts this list, and because of the strange, beautiful word he ends it on.

First, the setting. People are wondering if John might be the Christ, and he says no: "I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose." Then Jesus is baptized, and Luke adds a detail: Jesus was praying. "The heaven was opened, And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased." The voice has just said: my Son. And right there, before anything else happens, Luke drops in the genealogy. Matthew's Gospel has one too, but it begins with Abraham and runs forward, a story of Israel's kings. Luke's runs backward and doesn't stop at Abraham. It ends: "Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God." And in Genesis, Adam is also the name God gives to humankind, male and female together. So some readers hear Luke tying Jesus to every person who has ever lived, not one nation only, but the whole human family. And he's called Adam a son of God too. The voice at the river says this one is my beloved Son, and the list underneath says he belongs to everyone. The two lists don't match name for name between David and Joseph, and Christians have explained that in different ways: some say Luke follows Mary's family, others say adoption or old family custom explains it. The texts themselves don't say. What Luke does make plain is the shape: from the river all the way back to the garden.
screen: then, large: `WHICH WAS THE SON OF ADAM, WHICH WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of your grandparents' grandparents. Settle, and breathe. Start with your parents, or whoever raised you. Then their parents. Then one more step back, people you may never have known: names you've heard once, a village, an old photograph, or nothing at all. That's fine. Picture them anyway, eight people, sixteen, people who worked and worried and prayed or didn't, all so that you could be sitting here. Keep going back, past what anyone remembers, until it's just people, the human family Luke traces. If you pray, you can give thanks for the ones whose names are lost. If you don't, simply notice how long the line is. The bell holds the time.
Adam, the name Genesis gives both the first man and all humankind: Luke's family tree climbing back past Abraham, all the way to Adam, and one more rung, to God.
Your line: son of adam, son of god. Today, when someone gets on your nerves, remember that Luke's list runs through them too, all the way back. Day five hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Some churches read Luke's account of the baptism on the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, and some Christians point to Luke's genealogy as a sign that Jesus belongs to the whole human family.

fork.setup: you're Luke. the voice from heaven has just said "my beloved Son." what do you write next?
options: a family tree that runs all the way back to Adam.
fork.reveal: Luke places the genealogy right there, climbing from Jesus back to Adam, "the son of God."

original.note: Hebrew: Adam. in Genesis, the first man's name, and in Genesis 5:2 the name given to humankind.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long list of names nobody reads.
what it means: Luke ties Jesus not to one nation only but to the whole human family, back to Adam.
what a scholar hears: Luke places the list between the voice saying "my Son" and the desert test that begins "if thou be the Son of God."

notes: 'More than seventy names': Luke's list has about 77 generations depending on manuscript and counting. Confirm.
Explanations for the differences from Matthew (Mary's line; levirate marriage or adoption, as in Julius Africanus) summarized without ranking. Confirm.
Jesus praying at the baptism (3:21) is unique to Luke among the Gospels. Confirm.
Hebrew adam as 'human being' is a standard gloss.
The voice-quote begins mid-verse 21 ('the heaven was opened').

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens on 'Most family trees'; 'more than seventy names' (a count that varies by manuscript) and 'most readers skip' cut; 'a detail only he gives' and the 'only Luke' myth reworded to what the text says (3:21, quoted in KJV); the Adam etymology replaced by Genesis 5:2, where Adam names humankind, and the 'whole human family' reading attributed to some readers; practice no longer tells the listener what to feel; howItsDone softened.
